label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: Before I tell you how the factory worked
findings.why: The factory is the book's central idea and it is never said in plain words what it is (a team of AI agents?) before the tour starts, so a new reader cannot tell what they are being shown.

findings.quote: it still shows the hold of that night
findings.why: Hold and wake are used here and the plain definitions only arrive at line 41, after the reader has already stumbled.

findings.quote: The page shows what the files say. The files say we stopped. So the page says we stopped.
findings.why: Three short sentences in a row, and the Conductor speaks before the reader has been told who the conductor is.

findings.quote: Every one of its 58 beats is a page that moves
findings.why: Beats is unexplained jargon and a page that moves is not something I can picture; a non-programmer wants slide, simply.

findings.quote: every slide has a link, a history and a check before it goes out
findings.why: History and check mean version control and automated testing to a programmer, and nothing to me; it makes the tour feel written for developers.

findings.quote: *How to read the scenes:* they are dramatised.
findings.why: A label that tells the reader how to read, where a plain sentence from the narrator saying the lines are written for the book would do.

findings.quote: plan, go, done, clean, as planned
findings.why: A string of five bare words with no explanation of what each one marks, so the sentence about 162 records tells me nothing.

findings.quote: their read keys were published on purpose too
findings.why: Vaults, read keys and fingerprints are the densest jargon in the chapter, arrive in one paragraph, and make it feel like security work for programmers.

findings.quote: Read in order, they are the team talking.
findings.why: An instruction on how to read; the thought (the commits are the agents talking to each other) can be said as a plain fact.

findings.quote: The page and my register do not agree on the wakes
findings.why: Register and the mismatch of one count is bookkeeping a first reader skims, and it interrupts the stop before they get to the point.

findings.quote: every wake started by the clock
findings.why: Wake is used with no explanation on the first page that uses it; the sentence about the four parts is otherwise a clear, followable map.

findings.quote: That list is often shorter than you expect
findings.why: It guesses what the reader expects; the invitation itself, the one step I could take tomorrow, is the best thing here and needs no forecast.

findings.quote: with the talk team's machinery copied in, rule for rule
findings.why: Machinery, session, key and hand-off arrive in one paragraph with no definition, and the page reads as a project log for people who already run such teams.

findings.quote: when the build went red for everyone
findings.why: Build and went red are programmer shorthand, and hold on its own judgement leans on a definition that sits in another chapter.

findings.quote: The team lost an evening to the usage limit, which chapter 21 tells.
findings.why: The usage limit and the handover are told in lines 9 and 11 and sent to chapters 20 and 21 as well, so the page points elsewhere for what it half tells.

what_holds: 03b-the-day-at-a-glance.md: the four parts with hour ranges give me a map of the day in three short paragraphs, and the figure promises a picture I can follow.
03-the-tour.md: four stops, each with one picture, a few lines and one line from an agent, are characters I can follow; the Deck line about every rule costing somebody a slide is vivid.
03-the-tour.md: the closing Something to try is a step I could take tomorrow with something I already made.
03-the-tour.md: the Words for this page note that defines wake, conductor and hold in plain terms is exactly what I need, just too late.
notes: As a first-build finisher: I get that there is a team of agents that built a talk in a day, but the word factory is never pinned down in these pages, and the making-of page (94) feels like it is for programmers, so I would stop there. Would start tomorrow: only the Something to try, not the rest.
